cards.back: Utah treats pedestrians, highway workers, animal riders, farm gear without a cab, boards, skates, cycles, scooters, motorcycles and wheelchairs as vulnerable highway users.
cards.front: Who counts as a vulnerable highway user in Utah

cards.back: Deliberately distracting a vulnerable road user in order to threaten harm or push that person off the road can lead to a citation with points on the driving record.
cards.front: What happens for deliberately threatening a vulnerable road user off the road

cards.back: Deliberately distracting or forcing a vulnerable user off the road can bring a citation, record entry and points.
cards.front: What penalty follows forcing a vulnerable user off the road

cards.back: Bicycles on the road count as vehicles with the same rights and duties as cars.
cards.front: How does Utah treat bicycles ridden on the road

cards.back: Drivers yield to bikes at crossings and keep off marked bike lanes except to enter a drive, obey police or handle an emergency.
cards.front: When must drivers yield to bikes and stay out of bike lanes

cards.back: When passing any bicyclist or vulnerable user, Utah requires at least three feet of clearance.
cards.front: How much clearance must you leave when passing any vulnerable user

cards.back: A driver passing a person on a bicycle must leave at least three feet of space beside that rider.
cards.front: How much space beside a bicycle rider when passing

cards.back: Drivers dim headlights within five hundred feet when near bikes at night and check before opening doors or backing.
cards.front: What night and parking duties do drivers owe bicyclists

cards.back: A bike or moped may be passed only where sight lines allow, never blindly over a crest, curve, bridge, tunnel, crossing or within one hundred feet of them.
cards.front: Where is passing a bike or moped forbidden for lack of sight

cards.back: A bike brake must halt the machine within twenty-five feet from ten miles per hour, and night riders need white front, red rear and side visibility.
cards.front: What brake and night visibility must a bicycle have

cards.back: A bicycle ridden when lights are needed must show a white front light plus red rear and side reflectors that remain visible from far down the road.
cards.front: What lights must a bicycle show when lights are needed

cards.back: On sirens or flashing emergency signals, drivers must pull at once to the right edge and halt until the vehicle passes.
cards.front: What must you do when sirens or flashing emergency signals approach

cards.back: A driver meeting an emergency vehicle using sirens or flashing warning lights must promptly move to the right edge and halt until it goes by.
cards.front: What must a driver meeting a siren emergency vehicle do

cards.back: Near a stopped roadside vehicle with hazards or amber lamps, slow down, give space and move a lane away when safe.
cards.front: What must you do near a stopped roadside vehicle with hazards

cards.back: A driver coming upon a stopped roadside vehicle with flashing hazard lights must slow down, give generous room, and shift one lane away when it can be done safely.
cards.front: What must you do coming upon flashing hazard lights at roadside

cards.back: Ignoring the move-over rule and being convicted means a four-hour classroom course within ninety days or a ninety-day suspension.
cards.front: What follows conviction for ignoring the move over rule

cards.back: No vehicle may exceed eight and one-half feet in width, while farm tractors may reach nine feet.
cards.front: What is the width limit for vehicles and farm tractors

cards.back: Road vehicles are capped at fourteen feet high, forty-five feet for a single unit, and sixty-five feet for most other combinations.
cards.front: What height and length caps apply to road vehicles

cards.back: Loads may project at most three feet ahead and six feet behind the body, with side overhang barred on the left and capped at six inches on the right.
cards.front: How far may loads project ahead behind and to the sides

cards.back: Tractor-trailers favor the center lane on multilane roads, need far longer braking room and mislead judges of speed at crossings.
cards.front: Why do tractor trailers favor the center lane and need room

cards.back: A car at fifty-five miles per hour stops in about one hundred thirty to one hundred forty feet, while a loaded rig can need over four hundred feet.
cards.front: How do car and loaded rig stopping distances compare at speed

cards.back: Long rigs swing left first for a right turn, so followers must wait for the maneuver to finish rather than squeeze past.
cards.front: What should followers do when a long rig turns right

cards.back: Truck blind areas reach about twenty feet ahead, along both flanks by the cab, and up to two hundred feet behind.
cards.front: Where are truck blind areas around the rig

cards.back: A large truck hides vehicles directly ahead of its cab, along both sides near the cab, and far behind its trailer, so a car unseen in the truck mirror is unseen by the trucker.
cards.front: How do truck hidden zones relate to the mirror check

cards.back: If a driver cannot see the trucker in the side mirror, the trucker cannot see that driver.
cards.front: How can you tell the trucker cannot see you

cards.back: Before returning after passing a large rig, the passer must see its full front in the rear-view mirror.
cards.front: When is it safe to return after passing a large rig

cards.back: A driver should never pull directly ahead of a fast-moving heavy truck because the loaded truck needs a much longer distance to halt than a car does.
cards.front: Why must you never cut directly ahead of a fast truck

cards.back: Mobility permits and pedestrian vehicles can use highways under stated conditions without standard registration or licensing.
cards.front: What highway exception exists for mobility permits and pedestrian vehicles

cards.back: Riders under fifteen need supervision or a certificate for motor-assisted scooters, and such scooters stay off fast or wide roads and posted no-board areas.
cards.front: What age and place limits apply to motor assisted scooters

cards.back: Lane filtering past stopped traffic is allowed only on same-direction multilane roads or off-ramps capped at forty-five miles per hour, at fifteen miles per hour or less and only when safe.
cards.front: When is lane filtering past stopped traffic allowed

cards.back: Slow filtering past stopped cars on a motorcycle is allowed only on suitable multilane roads at very low speed, while weaving between moving cars remains unlawful.
cards.front: How does legal filtering differ from illegal splitting

cards.back: A motorcycle's flashing turn signal does not prove the rider will turn. Many motorcycle signals require manual cancellation, and the rider might have left one operating accidentally.
cards.front: Should you assume a motorcycle will turn when its signal flashes

cards.back: Drivers stay halted until a walker clears at least their half of the road, even without a marked crosswalk.
cards.front: How long must you stay halted for a walker

cards.back: A vehicle halted for a pedestrian must stay stopped until the walker has cleared at least the half of the roadway the driver occupies.
cards.front: When may a vehicle halted for a pedestrian proceed

cards.back: Walkers with a guide dog or white cane get a full stop, and walkers without sidewalks use the left shoulder facing traffic.
cards.front: What duties apply for guide dogs and walking without sidewalks

cards.back: Slow vehicles show an orange-red triangle when below twenty-five miles per hour, and horses get quiet wide passes without horn or revving.
cards.front: How should you handle slow triangles and horses on the road

cards.back: Street-legal ATVs and UTVs use single-lane-each-way roads, keep to fifty miles per hour or less and hug the far right with reflector when the limit is higher.
cards.front: Where and how fast may street legal all terrain machines travel

cards.back: Stock no larger than manufacturer size with at least two thirty-seconds inch tread, plus lamps, signals, mirrors, horn, windshield or eye cover, and speedometer belong on street-legal all-terrain machines.
cards.front: What equipment belongs on a street legal all terrain machine

cards.back: At crossings halt fifteen to fifty feet from the rail, never park within fifty feet, and never pass another same-direction car there.
cards.front: Where must you halt park and pass at rail crossings

cards.back: A driver told to stop for a rail crossing must halt within a short marked band before the nearest rail and must stay stopped while the red lights keep flashing.
cards.front: Where must you halt for a rail stop order

cards.back: Flashing rail lights or bells mean full stop until they end, and gates must never be bypassed while moving or closed.
cards.front: What do flashing rail lights bells and gates require

cards.back: A driver must never steer around, beneath, or through rail gates while they are moving or lowered.
cards.front: May you steer around moving or lowered rail gates

cards.back: Trains hold full priority over every road user, may come either way without schedule, and a loaded freight at fifty-five miles per hour can run over a mile to halt.
cards.front: What priority and stopping truth apply to trains

cards.back: A stalled car on train tracks must be emptied at once, and anyone escaping an oncoming train should run angled toward the train so wreckage flies away from them.
cards.front: What should you do if your car stalls on train tracks

cards.back: Light-rail crossings need full track clearance, waiting until gates lift and reds quit, with a flashing train emblem as caution only rather than a stop order.
cards.front: What is required at light rail crossings and train emblems
